prompts.projects.narrow.short: The topic “[topic]” is too broad. Suggest 5 narrower versions.
prompts.projects.narrow.detailed: Help me narrow the topic “[topic]” for a [type of work] of [length]. Suggest 5 options: for each, the wording, what exactly will be studied, which sources are needed, why it's interesting and what's hard about it. Mark which is most realistic to finish in [time].
prompts.projects.narrow.refine: I like option [number], but it's still broad. Narrow it one more step.
prompts.projects.narrow.check: My topic: [topic]. Can it be covered in [length]? What's too much in it?
prompts.projects.question.short: Write a research question for the topic: [topic]
prompts.projects.question.detailed: For “[topic]”, suggest 4 research questions of different types: “how”, “why”, “to what extent”, “what if”. For each: what's needed to answer it (data, sources, a survey, an experiment), and whether a student could realistically do it in [time].
prompts.projects.question.refine: Question [number] is too general. Make it specific and measurable.
prompts.projects.question.check: My question: [question]. Is it open? Can it be answered honestly without forcing a conclusion?
prompts.projects.plan.short: Make a work plan for a [type of work] over [time].
prompts.projects.plan.detailed: Make a work plan for a [type of work] on “[topic]”, due in [time]. Stages: choosing and narrowing the topic, finding sources, draft, revision, formatting, preparing to present. For each: what to do, how much time to allow, the expected result. Leave a buffer for the unexpected.
prompts.projects.plan.refine: I'm behind at the [stage] stage. Rearrange the plan so I still finish on time.
prompts.projects.plan.check: Here's what I've done so far: [done]. What's the most important next step?
prompts.projects.arguments.short: What are the arguments for and against: [thesis]?
prompts.projects.arguments.detailed: My thesis: [thesis]. Make a table: argument, for or against, which fact or data would support it, where such data are usually found. Don't invent figures or studies: if support is needed, write “find a source”.
prompts.projects.arguments.refine: The strongest argument against is [argument]. How can I address it honestly in my work?
prompts.projects.arguments.check: I found a source for argument [number]: [source]. Does it really support it?
prompts.projects.sources.short: Which sources should I look for on “[topic]”?
prompts.projects.sources.detailed: For a project on “[topic]”, list the types of sources worth finding: textbooks, academic articles, official statistics, interviews, media. For each: what to look for, which search terms to use, how to check reliability. Don't invent specific titles.
prompts.projects.sources.refine: I need sources in [language]. What search queries should I use?
prompts.projects.sources.check: Here's my source list: [list]. Which types are missing for a balanced piece of work?
prompts.projects.logic.short: Check the logic of my draft: [draft]
prompts.projects.logic.detailed: Read the draft and check its logic: does each section relate to the main question, are there jumps without transitions, repetitions, conclusions without evidence? Give a list of problems with their location. Don't rewrite the text. Draft: [draft]
prompts.projects.logic.refine: Suggest a different order of sections and explain why it's better. Don't touch the text itself.
prompts.projects.logic.check: I've rearranged the parts: [new outline]. Is the logic clear now?
prompts.projects.unclear.short: Find the parts of this text that are hard to understand: [text]
prompts.projects.unclear.detailed: Read the text as [audience] would. Find places where a reader might get lost: unexplained terms, long sentences, unclear “it” and “this”, missing steps in reasoning. For each, quote the fragment and explain what's unclear. Text: [text]
prompts.projects.unclear.refine: For fragment [number], suggest 2 clearer ways to say it without changing the meaning.
prompts.projects.unclear.check: I've rewritten the unclear part: [new version]. Is it clear now?
prompts.projects.theses.short: Pick out the 5 main points of my work: [text]
prompts.projects.theses.detailed: Write the key points of my work for a [talk, abstract or defence]: 5–7 points, each a single claim the work actually supports. Don't add anything that isn't in the text. Note which section each point comes from. Text: [text]
prompts.projects.theses.refine: Cut it down to the 3 points I can say in one minute.
prompts.projects.theses.check: My key points: [theses]. Which of them isn't backed up by the work?
prompts.projects.checklist.short: Make a checklist for checking a [type of work] before handing it in.
prompts.projects.checklist.detailed: Make a checklist for a [type of work] before submission. Sections: content (answers the question, evidence), structure, sources and citations, formatting, language, integrity (own words, AI help disclosed if required). Write items as yes-or-no questions.
prompts.projects.checklist.refine: Add these requirements to the checklist: [requirements].
prompts.projects.checklist.check: I've got “no” for items [items]. Where should I start fixing?
prompts.projects.defence.short: What questions might I get when presenting a project on “[topic]”?
prompts.projects.defence.detailed: Here's a summary of my work: [summary]. Write 10 questions I might be asked at the defence: 3 about method, 3 about conclusions, 2 about weak points, 2 about practical value. For each, hint what to draw on in the answer but don't write the answer.
prompts.projects.defence.refine: Ask me these questions one at a time like an examiner, and press me if my answer is vague.
prompts.projects.defence.check: My answer to a hard question: [answer]. Is it honest and to the point? What should I cut?

verify.projects.narrow: Check that the narrowed topic has sources you can actually get: a topic that's too narrow has nothing to build on.
verify.projects.question: A good question can't be closed with a single link. If the answer is easy to look up, it isn't a research question.
verify.projects.plan: Compare the plan with your teacher's requirements or guidelines: the structure is often set in advance.
verify.projects.arguments: Back up every argument with a source yourself. AI words things convincingly even when there are no facts behind them.
verify.projects.sources: Don't cite book or article titles from the AI's answer until you've found them yourself: it can make up ones that don't exist.
verify.projects.logic: You decide what to change. The AI may suggest a logical structure that isn't yours.
verify.projects.unclear: An AI reader isn't your teacher. If in doubt, ask a classmate to read the text.
verify.projects.theses: The key points must match what the work actually says. Check each one against the text.
verify.projects.checklist: The main checklist is your teacher's or department's requirements. Add them to the list.
verify.projects.defence: Prepare the answers yourself from your own work. Examiners notice memorised wording that isn't yours.
